title: Aryadeva
hookLine: Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on

cards: A great teacher is only half of a lineage. The other half is the person who listens closely enough to carry it after the teacher is gone. Nagarjuna had such a student: Aryadeva.
Tradition remembers him less for inventing a new idea than for taking his teacher's middle way out into the world and testing it, in debate halls, against rival schools, and in verses of his own.

teach.b: Tradition also calls him Kanadeva, explains the name as the one-eyed deva, and tells a legend to account for it.
Someone admired one of his eyes, so he took it out and gave it away, to show that the body isn't worth clinging to. It's a legend, told to make a point about letting go.
His book is the Four Hundred, verses that put Nagarjuna's emptiness to work against clinging: to permanence, to the body, to pleasure, to the self. One verse lays out a teacher's order.
First turn a student away from harmful actions.

teach.h: HARM, THEN SELF, THEN ALL VIEWS.
teach.b: Then, in the middle, away from the idea of a solid self. And last, away from every view at all. Even emptiness isn't a place to cling.

That's a teacher thinking about how a student actually grows: one step, then the next. Then a hard ending. A Chinese account of his life says a follower of a rival he had beaten in debate attacked him with a knife.
As he lay dying, Aryadeva told his own students not to chase the man, and spoke of the attacker with compassion. In that telling, the last thing he taught was the teaching itself, lived.
A student who carried it to the end.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, Aryadeva's Four Hundred verses are studied alongside Nagarjuna's works in the Madhyamaka curriculum, and teachers explain its verse on the order of teaching.

o: a king who gave land to Nagarjuna's monks
Nagarjuna's teacher, who first taught him emptiness
Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on

s: he was Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on.
in the legend, Aryadeva gave away one of his eyes
that is why tradition also calls him Kanadeva, the one-eyed god.
Aryadeva's verse says to cling to emptiness at the end
last of all, the student is turned away from every view. even emptiness is not a place to cling.

games.q: you're Aryadeva, struck down by a rival's follower. your students want to chase the attacker. what do you tell them?
o: catch him and bring him to justice.
let him go, and hold him with compassion.
forget him and debate his teacher again.
games.why: in the Chinese account, Aryadeva told his students not to chase the man, and spoke of him with compassion.

practice: Bring to mind one thing a teacher showed you, a way of cooking, of fixing something, of calming down, and ask how you do it now. What did you keep exactly as you were shown, and what did you test for yourself and change?
Rest there, noticing where you, like Aryadeva, took a teacher's way out into the world.

wordCard.voice: Aryadeva. Nagarjuna's student, who wrote the Four Hundred verses and, in a Chinese account, forgave the man who struck him down. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit name of Nagarjuna's student; tradition also calls him Kanadeva.

carryVoice: Your line: the student carries it. Every lineage needs someone listening that closely. Day nine hundred sixty.
